en.sup: Supplied in English. The Greek sets the time with a participle construction, a genitive absolute; 'while' makes that link explicit.

01.r: Places the events within a stated year.

02.r: A year of the emperor's rule, used as a date.

03.r: Opens a new section of the narrative.

04.r: The number of the year in Tiberius's rule.
04.n: Abbott-Smith records this word only in this verse.

05.r: The article; 'of' comes from the genitive case of the noun.

06.r: The period of Tiberius's rule as emperor.
06.n: Abbott-Smith defines it as 'rule, sovereignty' and records it in the New Testament only here. It comes from ἡγεμών, a leader or governor, and shares its root with the verb used next of Pilate's governing; the YLT's 'government' keeps that closer to view than 'reign'.

07.r: The emperor, named to date the events.
07.n: Abbott-Smith identifies him as the Emperor Tiberius and records the name in the New Testament only here.

08.r: The imperial title borne by Tiberius.

09.r: Pilate held the office of governor over Judea at that time.
09.n: Abbott-Smith's third sense, 'to be governor of a province', which he gives for this verse. It is a present participle in a genitive absolute: literally 'Pontius Pilate governing Judea'.

10.n: Abbott-Smith calls it the praenomen, the personal first name, of Pilate.

12.r: Greek puts the article before the name of the region; English does not.

13.r: The southern region, under Pilate's rule.
13.n: The lexicon in the brief describes it as the southern part of the country, below Samaria.

14.r: Adds the next ruler to the list.

15.r: Herod held the office of tetrarch over Galilee.
15.n: Abbott-Smith gives 'to be tetrarch'. The title is built from 'four' and 'rule', literally a ruler of a fourth part; the brief's lexicon does not say whether that sense still applied.

16.r: Greek puts the article before the name of the region; English does not.

17.n: Abbott-Smith explains the Hebrew name as 'the circle, district', and calls Galilee the northern region of Palestine in New Testament times.

18.r: Herod Antipas, the tetrarch of Galilee.
18.n: Abbott-Smith lists this verse under Herod Antipas, not Herod the Great.

19.n: Abbott-Smith distinguishes several men of this name and lists this verse under the tetrarch.

20.r: A light connective adding Philip to the list.

21.r: With 'his', marks Philip as Herod's own brother.
21.n: Greek says 'the brother of him'; English uses 'his' alone.

24.r: Philip held the office of tetrarch over the region named next.

25.r: The article belonging to 'region' at the end of the phrase.

26.r: One of the districts Philip ruled.
26.n: Abbott-Smith treats the word as an adjective, 'Ituraean', describing the region. Greek says literally 'the Ituraean and Trachonitian region'; this study, like the ASV, turns both adjectives into place names.

28.n: Abbott-Smith relates the name to τραχύς, rough, and describes it as a rough region south of Damascus.

29.r: The territory made up of the two districts.
29.n: In Greek this noun closes the phrase and covers both names. The KJV, Geneva, DRC and YLT attach it to Trachonitis alone.

30.r: Adds the last ruler to the list.

31.n: Abbott-Smith records the name in the New Testament only here.

32.r: Greek puts the article before the name of the district; English does not.

33.n: Abbott-Smith describes it as a district in the Anti-Lebanon.

34.r: Lysanias held the office of tetrarch over Abilene.
